1. All drill presses are made in China. A few will have "final assy" in the US/EU, but the type of casting work done for the base and table isn't done in volume in the US. Point being - don't get blinded by "made int he USA" without understanding what makes for a quality tool.

  2. If you don't have a run-out indicator, get one. You can get a cheap one for $20 - takes the guess work out of understanding your spindle accuracy. Take it into the store and check the display units, might be educational.

  3. I've got an expensive 80 lb drill press and a cheap 1200 lb mill. The 1200 lb mill cuts 100X better than the drill press. Point being: for tool stability and repeatability you can't get around the fact that the little drill presses can only do so much. Do you need a 1200 lb mill to do what you want to do? Probably not. Just understand a what a drill press should / shouldn't be used for and work within those bounds.

  4. Maintain your tools. One thing that I find: someone who buys an expensive tool will maintain it. Therefore, it will last a long time. But, that same person will buy a cheap tool and abuse it - then it fails. If they had taken the same care for the cheap tool as the expensive tool ... results would have likely been different.
